title: Likes, dislikes, attitudes and preferences
subtitle: I'm really into it, I can't stand it, I'd rather stay here
summary: Say how much you like or dislike things, agree with So do I and Me neither, and talk about what you prefer.

lesson.heading: From love to hate
rows: I **like** a lot of pop music.
like it, but not a lot
I'm **not very keen on** folk music.

lesson.heading: Agreeing and disagreeing about likes
lesson.text: To agree, repeat the same kind of verb: **So do I** after *like*, **So am I** after *am*, **So can I** after *can*. For negative sentences use **Neither do I** / **Neither am I**. **Me too** and **Me neither** are easy informal answers.

examples.text: *A:* I love rock music. *B:* **So do I.** / **Me too.**
*A:* I'm really into dance music. *B:* **So am I.** / *B:* Really? **I'm not.**
*A:* I can't stand classical music. *B:* **Neither can I.** / **Me neither.**
*A:* I hate opera. *B:* Really? **I love it.**

lesson.note: Other useful replies: Yeah, it's OK. Oh, I'm not very keen. Really? I quite like it.

lesson.heading: What comes after these verbs
lesson.text: Many of these verbs are followed by a **noun** or an **-ing form**.

lesson.heading: Attitudes and interests
lesson.text: Your **attitude to** something is how you think or feel about it. Your **interests** are the things you enjoy doing. If two people have the same interests, they **have a lot in common**; if not, they **have nothing in common**.

examples.text: My **attitude to** a lot of things has changed over the years.

examples.note: = I liked chips in the past but not now

examples.text: I used to play computer games, but now they **don't interest** me.
I used to go swimming a lot, but now I don't go **at all**.
examples.note: at all makes a negative stronger

examples.text: Mark and I used to have the same **interests**, but now we have nothing **in common**.

lesson.heading: get used to = become familiar with
lesson.text: **Get used to** something means become familiar with it. It is followed by a noun or an **-ing** form - never by an infinitive.

examples.text: It takes time to **get used to living** in a different country.
I didn't like my new glasses at first, but now I've **got used to** them.
I found the winters very cold at first, but you **get used to** it.

left.label: prefer X to Y (in general)
examples: *A:* Which do you **prefer** in general, tea or coffee?
*B:* I **prefer** coffee **to** tea in the morning.

right.label: would prefer / would rather (now)
right.text: **I'd prefer to** + verb means the same as **I'd rather** + verb.
examples: *A:* Which **would** you **prefer**, the cinema or the theatre?
*B:* I think **I'd prefer to** go to the cinema.
*B:* I think **I'd rather** go to the cinema.

lesson.text: Three easy mistakes to avoid: *prefer X **to** Y* (not *than*), *get used **to** doing* (not *to do*), and *I'm **interested** in* (not *I'm interest in*).

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase with how much the speaker likes the thing.

pairs.right: I like it, but not a lot

pairs.left: I'm not very keen on it

exercises.prompt: My sister loves Robbie Williams, but I can't ___ him.
The two boys have nothing in ___; they're completely different.
exercises.explanation: Have nothing in common = have no interests that are similar.

exercises.prompt: The others enjoyed the film, but I didn't like it at ___.
exercises.hint: (one word - it makes the negative stronger)
exercises.explanation: At all makes a negative stronger.

exercises.prompt: I love the cinema, but this particular film doesn't ___ me.
exercises.explanation: It doesn't interest me = I don't find it interesting.

exercises.prompt: Carole is really ___ modern art at the moment. Personally, I hate it.
exercises.explanation: Be into something is an informal way of saying you like it very much.

exercises.prompt: I ___ to love cheese, but I never eat it now.
exercises.explanation: Used to + verb = it was true in the past but not now.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Would you like to go out? *B:* I'd ___ stay here, actually.
exercises.explanation: I'd rather stay here = I'd prefer to stay here.

exercises.prompt: I didn't like raw fish at first, but I'm ___ used to it now.
exercises.explanation: Get used to something = become familiar with it.
Repeat the same verb: can in A, so can in B.
For a negative sentence we say Me neither or Neither do I.
A used am, so B answers So am I.
A used have got, so B answers So have I.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite with 'to': 'I like rugby more than football.'
exercises.explanation: Prefer X to Y - not ~~prefer X than Y~~.

exercises.statement: *A:* Do you like it in England? *B:* Yes, I'm getting used to live here.
exercises.explanation: I'm getting used to living here. Get used to is followed by a noun or the -ing form.

exercises.statement: If you say 'I don't mind the new building', you mean it's OK.
exercises.explanation: Correct. I don't mind = it's OK for me.
